paras: The threatened lynching of William Patrick was a series of reported mob threats in Indiana in 1888 against a man jailed for the killing of a bartender named Carter at Spencer. A June dispatch from Evansville said Patrick, held at Rockport, was in hourly danger of being lynched by his victim's kin, who had already dug his grave. No attack took place, and in October Patrick was sentenced to two years in the penitentiary.

According to the Indianapolis Journal's Spencer correspondent, Patrick, "a frequenter of saloons," shot William Carter, bartender for T. Keen, at about 10 o'clock on the night of May 16 after a quarrel. The Indiana State Sentinel gave a fuller account: Patrick threw a glass of beer at Carter, told him "I am going to kill you," and shot him; Carter died within half an hour after making a dying statement. The Sentinel described Carter as a quiet young man of good habits and Patrick as a habitual drinker considered dangerous when drunk, and it said the town was "much excited."

Patrick surrendered on the evening of May 18, and once he was in the Spencer jail "many threats of lynching were made." When rumors reached Sheriff Dyers that a mob would try to hang Patrick that night, the sheriff quietly took him from the jail to the train and lodged him in the Indianapolis jail. Speaking to a Journal reporter there, Patrick said he had been nearly crazy for a week and did not know what he had done.

On June 19 the sheriff of Owen County took Patrick back to Spencer for a trial set to begin the next day, saying he no longer feared violence. Four days later, an Evansville special to the Indianapolis Journal reported word from Rockport that Patrick, "confined in the county jail for a most heinous murder," was in hourly danger of being lynched. A strong extra guard had been posted at the jail, which the dispatch said might be assaulted at any moment, because the kindred and friends of his victim declared he would occupy a grave they had already dug. No report of an attack on the jail appears in the coverage.

The case of the State vs. Wm. Patrick went to a jury at Martinsville on Saturday, October 6, and Patrick was given two years in the penitentiary. Sheriff Paul then heard that Owen County citizens were displeased with so light a verdict and that a mob was organizing to come on Sunday night and "administer capital punishment." The sheriff left with his prisoner for Jeffersonville, and the mob did not appear.

The case appeared only in the white press, led by the Indianapolis Journal, which followed it from the shooting through the verdict in short specials and local items. The Journal reported each lynching threat flatly, as a reason for moving the prisoner, without comment on the would-be mob. The Evansville dispatch traveled further: the Journal printed it on June 24 and again on June 25, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran it the same day under "Everything Ready But the Corpse.", and Nebraska and Dakota papers carried it on June 26 as "Likely to Be Lynched."

These copies named neither the murdered man nor the town of the crime, and none gave the race of anyone involved. The Sentinel's Spencer letter sided with the dead bartender but said residents, tired of three murders in two years, would "give the law aid" in checking such crimes.

The Evansville dispatch placed Patrick in the jail at Rockport, while the Journal had reported four days earlier that he was returned to Spencer, in Owen County, for trial. No paper connects the two places, so the coverage does not show whether the Rockport report misplaced the Spencer prisoner. Printings also differ on the dispatch's date (June 23, 24 or 26) and on the bartender's first name, William in the earlier reports and John in two others.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Patrick
bases: Patrick, jailed on a murder charge, was repeatedly reported in danger of being lynched by a mob or by his victim's kin, but no attack on him is reported (A2, A7, A13).

No one was killed: the papers report threats of lynching against Patrick in May, June and October 1888, but he was guarded, moved and finally sent to the penitentiary (A2, A7, A13). The threats were made in retaliation for the killing he was charged with, but no mob is reported to have acted.

The June threat at Rockport rests on one Evansville dispatch, printed in the Indianapolis Journal and copied elsewhere (A7, A9, A10); the May and October threats come from Indianapolis Journal reports alone (A2, A13).

accounts.label: Evansville dispatch
accounts.gist: A report from Rockport said Patrick, jailed for murder, was in hourly danger of lynching, an extra guard was posted, and his victim's kin and friends had dug a grave for him.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal (Spencer case)
accounts.gist: After the Spencer murder, many lynching threats were made and the sheriff moved Patrick to Indianapolis; he was later taken back for trial, convicted, and again moved when a mob was said to be forming.

framing.detail: The Rockport dispatch ran nearly verbatim under 'Lynching Threatened', 'Everything Ready But the Corpse.' and 'Likely to Be Lynched'.
The Indianapolis Journal reported the threats and the sheriffs' removals of Patrick without comment, noting Owen County's displeasure at the light verdict.
The Indiana State Sentinel's Spencer correspondent called Carter 'quiet, inoffensive' and Patrick 'a dangerous man when intoxicated', while saying the people would 'give the law aid'.

versions.value: Spencer, Owen County, where Patrick was taken back for trial four days before the dispatch

conflicts.note: No paper links the Rockport report to the Spencer case; the name, the murder charge and the timing match, but the coverage does not show whether Patrick was at Rockport or whether the dispatch misplaced him.
The Indianapolis Journal's own special, printed June 24, is the earliest and is the better evidence for June 23.
The earlier and local-source reports say William.

Rockport per the dispatch, but the same-named prisoner had been returned to Spencer for trial four days earlier; location uncertain.

The June dispatch ran in at least four papers from 1888-06-24; the Patrick case drew coverage from May 18 to Oct. 9.

info: Evansville dispatch reporting the danger dated June 23, 1888 (Indianapolis Journal); other printings date it June 24 or June 26. The threat itself is undated.
The June dispatch places Patrick in 'the county jail' at Rockport, Ind.; the murder, the May threats and the start of trial were at Spencer, Owen County; verdict at Martinsville.
William (Wm.) Patrick, a painter, married with two children; threatened, not harmed. No paper gives his race.
Accused of shooting and killing a bartender named Carter (William Carter in most reports, John Carter in two) at a Spencer saloon on May 16, 1888; the dispatch calls it 'a most heinous murder'.
In June, 'the kindred and friends of his victim'; in May, an unnamed mob at Spencer; in October, citizens of Owen County, by the sheriff's information.
Sentenced to two years in the penitentiary; the reported mob did not appear and the sheriff left with him for Jeffersonville.
